## Idempotency first

A script that is safe to run twice is worth far more than a script that is fast to write once. Before automating a manual process, ask what happens if the script runs again against a system already in the target state — a good automation script checks state before changing it, rather than assuming a blank slate.

## Prefer explicit over clever

`Get-Something | Where-Object { ... } | ForEach-Object { ... }` reads clearly to the next person — often future me — who has to maintain it. Dense one-liners that chain many pipeline stages together save a few lines but cost far more time the next time something breaks and someone has to figure out which stage failed.

## Log what changed, not just that something ran

A script that only prints "Done" is much harder to trust in production than one that prints exactly what it found, what it decided to change, and what it actually changed. `-WhatIf` support and a real change log are worth building in from the start, not retrofitted after the first incident caused by a script that changed more than expected.

## Treat credentials as a first-class design constraint

Automation that "just works" by embedding a credential directly in a script is a liability the moment that script is shared, copied, or version-controlled. Deciding how a script authenticates — a managed identity, a credential store, an interactive prompt — is a design decision to make before writing the first line of logic, not an afterthought.

## Small, composable scripts over one large script

A single automation script that tries to do everything becomes the hardest thing in the environment to safely change. Several small, single-purpose scripts that can be tested and run independently are easier to reason about, easier to hand off, and easier to replace one at a time as requirements change.
